title: 7-free-way-to-check-whether-AI-search-engines-can-actually-see-your-website
html:
7 free ways to check whether AI search engines can actually see your website

Most site owners have run a Google PageSpeed test. Far fewer have checked whether ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google's AI Overviews can actually read, understand and cite their content. That's a different question, and increasingly a more important one.

Generative engine optimisation (GEO) is the discipline of making your website legible to AI systems rather than just crawlable by traditional search bots. The two overlap, but they're not the same thing — a page can rank perfectly well on Google while being invisible to an LLM that's summarising answers rather than indexing pages.

Here are seven free ways to check where you stand, roughly in order of how much each one actually tells you.

1. Google's Rich Results Test

This checks whether your structured data validates against Schema.org specifications. It's a useful first pass and it's free, but it only confirms that your markup is syntactically correct — not that it's complete, not that an AI crawler can reach it, and not that it covers the entity types that matter for GEO (Organization, Person, FAQPage and so on).

2. Schema.org's own validator

A second opinion on markup validity, useful for catching errors the Rich Results Test misses. Same limitation applies: it tells you your JSON-LD is well-formed, not that it's strategically useful.

3. View source vs rendered DOM

Open your homepage, view source, and compare it against what actually renders in the browser. If your schema, headings and core content only appear after JavaScript executes, many AI crawlers will never see them. This is the single most common reason a well-optimised-looking React or Vue site is invisible to generative search — the crawler sees an empty shell. It's free, it takes thirty seconds, and almost nobody does it.

4. Ask the AI directly

Query ChatGPT, Perplexity or Claude with a question your site should plausibly answer, and see whether you're cited. This is the most honest test there is, but it's also the least systematic — one favourable answer doesn't tell you why, and one bad answer doesn't tell you what to fix.

5. An llms.txt check

A growing number of sites now publish an llms.txt file at their root, signalling to AI crawlers what content is available and how it should be interpreted. Checking whether you have one — and whether it's accurate — is a five-minute task that most competitors still haven't done.

6. A manual entity audit

Does your About page clearly state who you are? Do you have consistent sameAs links connecting your website to your LinkedIn, Crunchbase or other verified profiles? AI systems build confidence in citing you through named entity recognition (NER) and corroboration across sources. A page with no entity signals is much harder for a model to trust, however well-written the content is.

7. A weighted, automated audit

Doing the above six manually is informative but slow, and none of them give you a single comparable score across visits. This is the gap CiteSite was built to close: a free, web-based tool that runs your URL through a weighted set of GEO dimensions — structured data coverage, server-side renderability, entity signals, content structure and more — and returns a score with specific, prioritised recommendations.

It doesn't replace the manual checks above; it consolidates them into one pass so you know where to focus first. There's no account required and no data is stored after your report is generated.

Where to start

If you only have ten minutes, do two things: view source on your homepage to check what's actually reaching crawlers, and run your URL through a free audit to get a structured baseline. Everything else on this list is worth doing eventually, but those two will tell you the most for the least effort.

html:
What is zero-click search? A complete 2026 guide

You rank on the first page of Google. Nobody visits your site.

This isn't a glitch. It's the defining dynamic of search in 2026 — and if your reporting still treats organic ranking as a reliable proxy for organic traffic, the numbers stopped making sense some time ago.

Zero-click search happens when a user's query is answered directly on the search results page, so completely that there is no reason to click anything. It has existed since Google introduced featured snippets in 2014, but it has accelerated dramatically with the rollout and expansion of AI Overviews, AI Mode and now persistent search agents. Understanding what drives it, what it means for content strategy and what to do about it is no longer optional for anyone working in organic search.

This guide covers the mechanics, the data, and the practical response.

What zero-click search means

A zero-click search is any query that ends on the search results page without the user clicking through to a website. The user asked a question; the search engine answered it. Job done — from Google's perspective. From yours, a potential visit never happened.

Zero-click searches are not new. They became a serious concern for content teams around 2019, when Google began aggressively expanding featured snippets, knowledge panels and answer boxes. What changed in 2024 and 2025 was scale: the launch of AI Overviews transformed the featured snippet from an occasional occurrence into a near-universal layer on top of the results.

The difference between a featured snippet and an AI Overview

A featured snippet pulls a passage from a single ranking page and displays it above the results. The source is cited, the format is constrained, and the original page is still just one click away with a visible link.

An AI Overview is something different. It synthesises information from multiple sources into a generated answer, often with supporting links but no single prominent source. It can run to several paragraphs, include lists and tables, and address follow-up angles the user hadn't yet typed. It is designed to be sufficient on its own.

That sufficiency is exactly what drives zero-click behaviour. When an answer is complete, the incentive to click disappears.

The 2026 data: how bad is it?

The short version: worse than most teams have acknowledged, but more nuanced than the headline numbers suggest.

SISTRIX published click-through rate data in March 2026 showing position one CTR had fallen from 27% to 11% in twelve months. That 16-percentage-point drop is the sharpest year-on-year decline in recorded CTR history for the top organic position.

The query-level data is equally stark:

  • 60% of all Google queries now end without a click
  • 69% of news-related searches result in zero clicks
  • 93% of queries made through Google AI Mode end without a click

When an AI Overview specifically appears above the results, the zero-click rate for that SERP jumps to 83%, and the page ranking first loses approximately 58% of the clicks it would otherwise receive.

See the full zero-click statistics for 2026

The nuance the headlines miss

None of the above means traffic has become worthless. Research from First Page Sage shows that visitors arriving via AI-referred sources convert at 4.4 times the rate of traditional organic visitors. The traffic that does make it through is better qualified, more intentional and more commercially valuable than average organic traffic.

The picture, properly framed, is this: fewer visits, higher quality per visit. The problem is that most analytics setups are not measuring visit quality — they are measuring visit volume. That is the reporting gap that most urgently needs closing in 2026. How to measure success when clicks disappear

What is driving zero-click growth in 2026

Three distinct mechanisms are accelerating zero-click behaviour this year. Each matters for a slightly different strategic reason.

1. Google AI Overviews at scale

AI Overviews — powered by Gemini 3.5 Flash as of June 2026 — now appear on a significant and growing share of all Google queries globally. Unlike their 2024 pilot phase, AI Overviews in 2026 are no longer limited to informational queries. They appear on commercial queries, comparison queries and increasingly on navigational ones.

Google's June 2026 core update specifically targeted what it called "information extractability and citation-worthiness" as ranking signals — a clear signal that the search engine is actively building infrastructure for its AI answer layer, not just bolting it on.

2. AI Mode as the default for complex queries

Google's AI Mode — a full-session AI interface that replaces the traditional results page for multi-step or conversational queries — became the default experience for complex searches in mid-2026. Ninety-three percent of AI Mode sessions end without a click to an external site. For users who adopt AI Mode as their primary search interface, the traditional click-through is becoming a deliberate exception rather than an automatic next step.

3. Google information agents: the next frontier

The most significant long-term driver of zero-click behaviour is one that most content teams have not yet grappled with: Google's information agents.

Announced at Google I/O 2026 and available to AI Ultra subscribers from 12 June 2026, information agents operate in the background, monitoring the web continuously on a user's behalf across their priority topics. A user who sets up an agent to track "best project management tools for agencies" will receive synthesised updates from that agent — without ever performing a search.

The implication for content: discovery is increasingly delegated. If your content is not the kind that an AI agent will surface in a background summary, you may not exist in the user's world at all — regardless of where you rank.

What zero-click search means for your content strategy

The temptation in the face of these numbers is to retreat: reduce content investment, focus on brand channels, wait and see. That response misreads the data.

The right response is to shift the goal of content from generating clicks to generating citations.

Being cited within a Google AI Overview drives 120% more organic clicks than appearing on the same search results page without a citation. The mechanism is counterintuitive but consistent: an AI Overview that cites your content signals to users that you are an authoritative source, making the click to your site more intentional and more likely to convert.

This shifts the core question from "how do I rank higher?" to "how do I get cited?". The answers overlap substantially — authority, trust signals and content quality matter in both cases — but the tactical implications diverge in important ways.

Content that survives zero-click search

Not all content is equally vulnerable. Analysis of LLM citation patterns shows that certain content types are cited by AI engines far more often than others:

  • Original research and proprietary data: First-party findings that no AI can synthesise from existing web content are consistently cited. Trend and analysis posts attracted LLM citations 78% of the time in one large-scale study; generic educational how-to content sat at 12%.
  • First-person experience and case studies: Accounts that are grounded in real experience cannot be replaced by aggregated summaries. AI engines cite them precisely because they contain information that isn't available elsewhere.
  • Expert opinion and commentary: A named expert with verifiable credentials saying something substantive provides exactly the kind of EEAT signal AI systems are trained to surface.
  • Timely original reporting: Fresh content gets cited approximately 4.3 times more often than content older than three months. Speed and recency matter even more under AI-mediated search than they did under traditional SEO.

7 content types that survive zero-click search

Content that is most at risk

Conversely, some content categories face genuine structural headwinds:

  • Generic how-to guides: If the answer can be assembled from publicly available information, an AI Overview will assemble it. Commodity instructional content is exactly what AI Overviews are best at replacing.
  • Listicles based on aggregated sources: "Best tools for X" roundups built from other roundups are the clearest example of content an AI can generate on demand.
  • Thin informational pages targeting featured snippets: The entire strategy of writing content calibrated to win a featured snippet now feeds directly into AI Overview training data. The snippet win that drove traffic in 2022 may be fuelling a zero-click answer in 2026.

The platform fragmentation problem

One feature of zero-click search in 2026 that many strategies miss: it is not a single ecosystem. Google, ChatGPT, Perplexity and other AI search platforms each operate independent citation networks with minimal overlap.

Research shows that only 11% of domains are cited by both ChatGPT and Perplexity. A brand that has successfully optimised for Google AI Overviews has no statistical guarantee of appearing in ChatGPT Search results, and vice versa.

This matters because users increasingly spread their search behaviour across platforms. A content strategy that focuses exclusively on Google AI Overview eligibility is leaving significant AI search real estate unaddressed.

GEO vs SEO: optimising for citations, not clicks

FAQ

Is zero-click search the same as a featured snippet?

No, though they are related. A featured snippet is a specific format — a box pulled from a single webpage — that predates zero-click as a widespread phenomenon. Zero-click search is the broader behaviour: any query answered on the results page without the user visiting a site. AI Overviews are now the primary driver of zero-click behaviour, having largely superseded featured snippets as the dominant answer-surface on Google.

Does zero-click search mean content marketing is dying?

No. The relationship between content and discovery has changed, but content remains the raw material that AI systems draw on to generate answers. The difference is that the goal has shifted from generating clicks to generating citations. Content that earns AI citations can drive more valuable traffic than traditional ranked content, because AI-referred visitors convert at significantly higher rates than average organic visitors.

Can small sites compete for AI citations?

Yes, and in some ways more easily than for traditional rankings. Research shows that 90% of ChatGPT citations come from pages not ranked in Google's top 20. The citation signal that AI engines respond to is content quality, credibility and specificity — not domain authority in the traditional sense. A specialist publisher with deep, original, well-structured content can outperform a large general-interest site in AI citation frequency.

How do I know if my site is being cited in AI Overviews?

The most reliable method is direct monitoring: run your priority queries in Google AI Mode regularly and check for citations. Tools including the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit and Ahrefs Brand Radar now track AI citation frequency across major platforms automatically. You should also look for a +120% CTR differential on queries where you hold an AIO citation versus queries where you rank but are not cited. full guide to measuring GEO performance

Will Google's information agents make zero-click search even worse?

For traffic volume, probably yes. Google's information agents, available from June 2026, monitor topics continuously in the background without users needing to search. Discovery becomes delegated, and the explicit search — the moment that generates a click — may never happen. The compensating factor is that content surfaced by agents to high-intent users may drive very high-quality visits when clicks do occur. The priority is ensuring your content is the kind that agents will surface at all.

Conclusion

Zero-click search is not a temporary aberration or a problem Google will walk back. It is the direction search is moving, driven by the same user preference for immediate answers that made featured snippets successful in the first place. AI Overviews, AI Mode and information agents are each expressions of that preference at increasing scale.

The right response is not to abandon content investment. It is to redirect it: from content optimised to rank toward content worthy of citation. Original research, first-person expertise, timely analysis and deeply structured information are the foundations of both.

The click was always a means to an end. The end — reaching the right people at the moment they need what you offer — is still entirely achievable. The path there has changed.

title: GEO as a threat surface
excerpt: New research shows that deep research agents can be "poisoned" to shift what gets cited.
html:
Seven months ago, 76% of the pages Google cited in AI Overviews came from the organic top 10.

That figure is now 38%.

We've been talking about the gap between rankings and AI visibility for a while. But this rate of collapse — in under a year — is something I don't think most SEO teams have fully reckoned with yet. Ranking well and being cited in AI answers are becoming genuinely separate disciplines, requiring different signals, different content structures and different measurement entirely.

It gets more interesting. Only 17% of AIO citations currently come from the organic top 10 at all. Which means the other 83% of what AI Overviews cites is coming from somewhere your rank tracker isn't watching.

Then this week a new arXiv paper added a dimension I haven't seen discussed much in the industry. Researchers demonstrated that deep-research AI agents can be "poisoned" via manipulated user-generated content — Reddit threads, forum posts, reviews — to shift what gets cited and recommended. The authors frame it explicitly as the generative-AI equivalent of black-hat SEO.

So GEO is no longer just an opportunity. It's also a threat surface.

Brands that are invisible in AI answers right now aren't just missing traffic. They're leaving a vacuum that others — including bad actors — are already working out how to fill.

The question I keep coming back to: how many teams are building a GEO strategy at all, let alone a defensive one?

title: E-E-A-T: The credibility layer
excerpt: Most discussions of AI search optimisation focus on what machines can read: structured data, heading hierarchies, metadata. But there's a layer underneath all of that — one that determines whether an AI system considers your content credible enough to cite in the first place. That layer has a name: E-E-A-T.
html:
Why AI search needs humans to decide what's worth quoting

Most discussions of AI search optimisation focus on what machines can read: structured data, heading hierarchies, metadata. But there's a layer underneath all of that — one that determines whether an AI system considers your content credible enough to cite in the first place. That layer has a name: E-E-A-T.

What E-E-A-T actually is

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It originates in Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines — a document used to train human evaluators who assess whether pages genuinely serve users well. The framework gained its first "E" (Experience) in December 2022, reflecting a growing emphasis on first-hand knowledge over secondhand aggregation.

The four signals work as a hierarchy, but Trust sits at the top. A page can appear experienced and authoritative and still fail if the underlying content is inaccurate, anonymous, or lacking clear provenance.

The human-in-the-loop you didn't know about

Here's where it gets interesting from an AI perspective. E-E-A-T is not an algorithm. It is a framework applied by human quality raters — contractors who manually review pages and score them against Google's guidelines. Their assessments don't directly affect individual rankings, but they feed into how Google trains and calibrates its ranking systems over time.

This makes E-E-A-T one of the clearest examples of human-in-the-loop design in production AI. The outputs of these evaluations shape what the model learns to reward — meaning the entire edifice of AI-generated search results rests, in part, on human judgement about what trustworthy content looks like. That's a meaningful architectural choice, and it has practical implications for how you build content.

What it means for AIO

The signals that quality raters look for map almost directly onto what AI Overviews and answer engines use when deciding what to cite. Clear authorship. Named expertise. Transparency about methodology, sources, and perspective. Content that demonstrates the author has actually done the thing rather than synthesised it from elsewhere.

This last point — Experience — is where the most recent updates have added pressure. Generic, abstract content that reads as competent but impersonal is increasingly scrutinised. Content with clear first-hand grounding: dated accounts, named locations, specific outcomes, attributed perspectives — this is what both human raters and the systems they train are looking for.

The practical implication: treat your About page, author bio, and any methodology you describe not as supporting material, but as core E-E-A-T infrastructure. These are the signals that tell both humans and machines whether your content is worth quoting — or merely worth reading.

One important nuance: E-E-A-T is an evaluative framework, not a direct ranking signal. You cannot "add E-E-A-T" to a page the way you add schema markup. What you can do is ensure the signals it looks for are present, visible, and honest.

title: From SEO to GEO: Why JSON-LD Is the Hidden Layer Behind AI Visibility
excerpt: Learn about the importance of JSON-LD schema for making websites discoverable by generative AI platforms.
html:
JSON-LD schema has quietly become one of the most important tools for online discoverability — not just for search engines, but for AI systems and large language models (LLMs) as well.

In simple terms, JSON-LD is structured data that helps machines understand what your website content actually means. Rather than forcing AI systems to “guess” whether a page is about a product, article, organization, or service, schema provides explicit context. That clarity is increasingly valuable in the era of AI-generated answers and conversational search.

Modern LLMs don’t just scan keywords. They look for signals of authority, relevance, and structure. Well-implemented schema helps these systems identify:

  • Who your business is
  • What your pages are about
  • Which content is authoritative
  • How different pieces of information connect together

The result? Improved discoverability, more accurate AI summaries, and a greater chance of being surfaced in generative search experiences.

For businesses investing heavily in content, failing to implement structured data is like publishing a book without chapter titles. Your information may still exist online, but AI systems are far less likely to interpret it correctly or prioritize it confidently.

This is especially important when combined with emerging GEO practices such as llms.txt files. While llms.txt helps guide AI systems toward your preferred content and positioning, JSON-LD schema provides the semantic structure that helps those systems understand your site at a deeper level. Together, they create a stronger foundation for AI visibility.

The technical setup itself is relatively straightforward. The real value lies in strategy: choosing the right schema types, aligning them with your authority goals, and ensuring AI systems consistently interpret your brand the way you intend.

That’s where a professional GEO audit becomes valuable. Many websites already have schema installed — but very few are truly optimized for AI-driven discovery.

title: The importance of having an llms.txt file
excerpt: Why you need an llms.txt file if you're serious about GEO discoverability.
html:
An llms.txt file might sound niche today, but it’s quickly becoming a critical part of modern SEO and GEO strategy. As AI-driven search tools like OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and other large language models increasingly shape how users discover information, websites need clearer ways to communicate with these systems.

Think of llms.txt as a guidebook for AI. It helps language models understand which parts of your site matter most, which content is authoritative, and how your information should be interpreted. While traditional SEO focused on search engine crawlers, GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) is about influencing how AI systems summarize, cite, and recommend your brand.

A strong llms.txt file typically includes:

Your preferred site description and expertise areas Key URLs and priority content sections Citation preferences and canonical resources Guidance on structured content or documentation Instructions that reduce AI confusion or hallucination risks

The goal isn’t just visibility — it’s accuracy. Without clear signals, AI tools may misunderstand your content, overlook valuable pages, or fail to associate your brand with the topics you want to own.

Implementation itself is relatively simple, but strategy is where most businesses fall short. The real challenge is deciding what AI systems should prioritize and how that aligns with your broader SEO, content, and authority-building efforts.

That’s why forward-thinking brands are beginning to audit their sites specifically for AI discoverability, not just search rankings. An llms.txt file is no longer a “future-proofing” exercise — it’s becoming part of building a resilient online presence in the AI era.

If you’re unsure whether your website is truly optimized for AI-driven discovery, a professional GEO audit can reveal gaps traditional SEO tools often miss.

title: What Is Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO)?
excerpt: GEO is the practice of optimising your content to be cited by AI-powered search engines and large language models. Here's what you need to know.
html:
What is GEO — and why does your website need it?

Search has changed. When someone types a question into Google, ChatGPT, or Perplexity today, they often receive a direct answer — synthesised, confident, and sourced from a handful of trusted pages. Your website may rank on page one and still be invisible in that response. That's the problem GEO is designed to solve.

Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO) is the practice of structuring your website so that AI-powered search engines can understand, trust, and cite your content. Where traditional SEO focuses on getting pages to rank, GEO focuses on getting content to be used — pulled into AI Overviews, featured in chatbot responses, and quoted by the large language models that an increasing proportion of your potential audience now relies on for answers.

Why it matters right now

AI search adoption is accelerating rapidly. Tools like Google's AI Overviews, Perplexity, and ChatGPT Search are reshaping how people find information — and they are highly selective about their sources. Pages that lack clear structure, authoritative signals, and machine-readable context are simply passed over, regardless of their traditional search ranking.

GEO isn't a replacement for SEO. It's the next layer. And the websites that get ahead of this shift now will hold a significant advantage as AI-mediated discovery becomes the norm.

What a GEO audit covers

A proper GEO audit examines how well your site communicates with AI systems — from your structured data and metadata to your content architecture, entity signals, and crawlability. It identifies exactly where you're losing visibility and what to do about it.
